toc.title: Hypervigilance has a tinge of freeze
A panic flavor or a rage flavor
Memories and numbness feed each other
Don't sacrifice your safety for the goal
Regulation is ongoing, not just for crises

blocks.p: Please put yourself first with this one. It's all about sexual trauma and intimacy, and it's potentially pretty triggering, so take a break if you need to. These are my thoughts, not specific life advice for the person who wrote to me or for anybody else.
A listener wrote in with this question:

q: I've been listening to your podcast for a long time now and am just coming into the realization that I think I experienced childhood sexual abuse. I think I'm in perpetual shutdown and hypervigilance somehow. It feels like intimacy is sometimes impossible, and other times I feel like a different person. I wonder if you had any thoughts on how to regulate when a lot of what I'm remembering and putting together still makes me numb and unfeeling. I hope this isn't too much to ask. I'm aware you can't give in-depth advice, et cetera, and I'm seeing a psychotherapist at the moment.

blocks.p: Good for you for seeing someone. And you're right, I can't give in-depth advice. But I'll give my thoughts, and hopefully they're helpful. I want to address a few of the pieces she laid out, in chunks.

blocks.h: Hypervigilance has a tinge of freeze

blocks.p: First, the perpetual shutdown and hypervigilance. In my opinion, what I see in hypervigilance is freeze: the flight or fight state active along with the shutdown state.

I think there's a bit of shutdown in hypervigilance because there's some immobility. When you're hypervigilant, you're kind of frozen in place, stuck in place, but aware. I think of the stereotypical image of the child who hears the keys outside the door: the abusive father is coming home. That triggers them to be very still and frozen in place, but also really revved up, like they want to run away, maybe fight.

That's how I understand hypervigilance. We're keenly aware of even the smallest details in the environment that are potential dangers, and there's a suspense in there, a freeze element. When there's danger, you pause. You're still, you're immobile. But with hypervigilance, you're stuck in that immobility while you're also ready to run away, and possibly to fight.

blocks.h: A panic flavor or a rage flavor

blocks.p: Hypervigilance could have something to do with panic, maybe even rage. With panic, there's that immobility while highly charged up. Shutdown is part of freeze, so that goes together for me.

But I think there could be an element of rage in hypervigilance too. It's that constant scanning of the environment, looking for danger. That could be someone in flight, who wants to get away from the danger. But it could also be someone in a stuck fight state who is also scanning for danger, not consciously, and then lashes out at anything they perceive to be a threat.

So in a way they're opposites. One person wants to get away from the danger, but they're immobile. The other wants to aggress upon the danger, and they're also in this immobility, frozen, but then explosive. That anger, that rage, that fight energy is frozen inside of them. When they detect a threat, instead of freezing and getting smaller, hiding, or wanting to run away and then panicking, they explode in rage.

Either way, someone who's hypervigilant is kind of always in that immobile but scanning for danger mode. The potential for that state to be triggered is always there, with a panic flavor or more of a rage flavor.

The perpetual shutdown makes sense, because that energy is frozen into the system. This is extremely common for someone with a history of sexual trauma. They probably had an impulse to run away or fight while being immobilized, and they may have been forced to immobilize.

That's what trauma is. There are two paths to trauma. The first is surviving an acute life threat, where you're forced to immobilize, or perceive you have to immobilize, while highly charged to run away or fight. The second is the chronic disruption of connectedness, where your impulse to connect with safe others is constantly being severed. That can lead to a stuck, traumatized state as well.

When we say childhood sexual trauma, I'm assuming that means multiple events, not one event. That means there were probably multiple events of being immobilized while in flight or fight. There's an element of shutdown in a single event, and with repeated events there's definitely going to be an element of shutdown. But over a longer period of time, that person's potential to exist in a shutdown, disconnected, numb state is probably going to increase.

So I could see someone existing in shutdown, or in a very hypervigilant, panicky freeze state, or fluctuating between the two. Maybe they exist more in a shutdown state, but that freeze energy is in there, and when it gets triggered it may look like hypervigilance, or panic, or rage, whatever it is for that individual person.

These states don't have to be either/or. It's not like you're just in flight, just in fight, just in shutdown, or just in freeze. There can be ladder climbing up and down, or a fluctuation between two states. Maybe someone can come out of shutdown, but has a really hard time with their fight energy, so staying in that fight energy and using it to keep climbing the ladder is a big challenge. They might spend a lot of time in both of those states.

So yes, intimacy is going to be challenging, absolutely. At least in part, this could be because immobilization is part of sexual intimacy. There's a lot of movement involved in sex, but there's also some immobility.

If someone has hypervigilance, with a rageful flavor or a panicky flavor, the body needs movement. If we want to run away or fight, we need movement. With freeze energy going on, there's immobility, and the body needs to move. So immobilizing when you're really highly revved up may not go over very well. And when it comes to physical intimacy, being immobile is kind of a part of that. If you go into that situation with a lot of flight or fight energy in your system, without being able to handle it or mindfully feel it, that may be too much. Now you're immobilizing yourself, and your system needs movement. It needs to run away, or use aggression to solve a situation.

I'm not talking about sex there. I'm talking about the flavor that's stuck in the system from that person's history. Especially from childhood sexual abuse or any sexual trauma, there's probably some unresolved flight or fight energy still in the system that got frozen due to the immobility, and that never got to complete the response to run away or to fight. If you immobilize yourself while that's triggered, it's just re-traumatizing. It doesn't actually help.

Ideally, sex is a cue of safety. Ideally, physical intimacy is something we share with somebody. We allow ourselves to feel vulnerable or exposed, to feel trust, to feel connection. But it may not always be that. Sometimes it's not a safe experience, and we may not be accessing our safe and social state. That may be because immobility is too much.

Being still requires that we're immobile but okay with it. Not just okay with it mentally or cognitively, but with our safety pathways actually active along with the shutdown pathways. That's called stillness. Without the safety pathways active, it's more of a defensive immobility.

Play requires the same thing: the safety pathways active along with the flight and fight pathways. We're mobile, but in our safety pathways and able to co-regulate and connect with people while we play.
Physical intimacy has elements of both play and stillness. And you can't play, and you can't be still, unless your safety pathways are active.

Trauma is the inability to access your safety pathways. You're stuck in more of a defensive state. So for anybody in more of a traumatized state, a situation where they're immobilizing might be really hard. A situation with a playful element, a social element, vulnerability, and trust is going to be a big challenge, because their safety pathways are just less active than someone who's not in a traumatized state.

Put all of that together: the context of sexual contact, the element of immobility, and a traumatized state from childhood sexual abuse. It may be a really tall order to engage in physical intimacy and be okay with it. If the familiarity is too much, or the safety isn't active enough, the vagal brake comes off. The safe and social state is the vagal brake. If it's not active, the result is too much flight or fight activation, too much defensive mobility, and that person is in more of a defensive state.

blocks.h: Memories and numbness feed each other

blocks.p: She said the memories make her feel numb and unfeeling. Yes, memories can make you numb and unfeeling. But the feelings of numbness, disconnection, and loneliness bring up memories as well. They feed into each other.

Once these memories, feelings, and thoughts become reintegrated in some way, once that stuck defensive energy is discharged (not the memories discharged, but the energy), once there's more of a vagal brake established, once we do this trauma healing or getting unstuck, whatever you want to call it, then however we got traumatized, the way we approach it will probably change.

That's true for anything, not just sex. If you're in a stuck defensive state after losing someone unexpectedly, once you process that grief, the next holiday without them is probably going to be a much different experience. Your mindset around it, the way you feel about it, who you allow into your life that day, all of that changes.

It's the same with physical intimacy. Once you reintegrate those feelings and memories, once you get unstuck, sex will be approached differently too. Instead of being a fearful thing, which it might be right now, or more anxiety producing, it might become a more connected, more shared, more vulnerable experience. The way you bring yourself to it will change significantly.

She asks how to regulate through the dysregulation. No matter how we got to a traumatized state, we have to identify safety. We have to identify what brings us to safety, what safety feels like, and increase our capacity to stay in a safety state, in those safety feelings and that vulnerability.

Confronting these things head-on can be helpful, but it could also easily be too much and be re-traumatizing. I don't recommend that personally. Just thinking about things that are familiar to what you survived can be re-traumatizing, if you're not ready for it, if your safety state isn't active enough. It can trigger all this stuff, and it just opens the wound without helping it heal. Simply sharing the story can be re-traumatizing, even with a therapist, if it happens before you're ready and they can't help you through it.

So if you try to engage in an act that's similar enough to what you went through, that can definitely be re-traumatizing as well. You have to build a safety state first, and then address the past if you want to. Maybe then you address it head-on. If you're terrified of spiders, maybe you do some vagal brake work, and then jump into a pit of spiders or something. It sounds terrible. Oh my God.

blocks.h: Don't sacrifice your safety for the goal

blocks.p: We all want a healthy sex life. Or fill in the blank for yourself: "I want to do whatever it is, but my stuck traumatic state doesn't allow me to." I would encourage people not to sacrifice their well-being and their feelings of safety in an attempt to reach that goal. The goal can still happen. I want you all to have whatever your hearts desire. But take your own inventory and ask yourself, "Am I ready for this?"

Here's a stereotypical example. A soldier comes back from war in a very traumatized state. Loud sounds, like a car backfiring, trigger their PTSD. That person might want to go to a shooting range, but those sounds might be too much. It might trigger their own stuck freeze state, and they go into a panic, and it re-traumatizes them. They want to do it, but they're not quite ready yet.

Take that example and apply it to yourself. Yes, we want a healthy sex life. Yes, we want to go to the shooting range, whatever it is. But you might not be there quite yet, and you have to be really honest with yourself about that. If you're constantly putting yourself into situations that re-traumatize you, you might not be helping at all. You may be making it worse.
You can still have your goal. It is possible to have a better sex life, or go to the shooting range, or hold a spider. You might not be there yet, and that's okay. You have to find safety first.

blocks.h: Regulation is ongoing, not just for crises

blocks.p: Regulation is not a one-time thing. It's not only something you do as crises arise. It's an ongoing process, and building your ventral vagal safety state, the strength of your vagal brake and your social engagement system, is slow.
Don't wait until the crisis to do some regulation. Do these things beforehand. I think that's true for all of us. Work on your self-regulation before the crisis.
And do it a bit at a time, not all at once. We don't want to overwhelm your system more than it can handle. Gradual exposure, and then bit by bit, work your way to your goal.
I've shared before that I have a fear of heights. It's pretty general, but it's worst in my car when I can't see over the edge, like driving on a mountain cliff.

That came up on a drive to Yosemite, on a windy road with an awful, awful cliff. I know for my system that one section is too much. So I asked my wife, "Hey, do you mind driving this section? I just can't handle it. I'm not there yet."

But as I've continued to do my own work, other sections of that drive that were challenging the last time we were there, ones that also had cliffs, though not as extreme, were a lot easier this time. Before, they were a trigger for me, and I felt that panicky flavor come up. This time I thought, "Oh, I don't feel it this time." I was way more regulated. I was able to talk with my wife and the kids, listen to music, sing. I was fine.

So little by little, I've been working on this fear of heights while driving, and I noticed a significant difference. But there's still that one cliff that's too much for me. Even thinking about it, I could feel a little of that freeze energy. That's not a bad thing, and maybe I could have rolled through it. But I made the decision not to push my way through. I'm going to compile my wins.

That's what I want you to do as well. Instead of jumping into whatever it is, go bit by bit, with gradual exposure. Build up those wins, that success, that confidence. Really, it's building up the strength of your vagal brake so you can handle the next challenge.

So ask yourself what you can tolerate. If your sex life is a challenge for you, what can you tolerate? Can you tolerate simple touch? Some people may have a hard time with that. Take your own inventory and ask:

ul: Do I actually feel safe with this person?
Is there co-regulation happening with this person?
Can I handle (fill in the blank)?

blocks.p: Be honest with yourself. Little by little, no matter what it is, can help. Then build from there. Notice what it feels like to be successful. Notice what it feels like to have a little more safety in your system, little by little, until you get to where you want to be. And then challenge yourself with something else.
